promise: After this you can explain what an autoscaler does, how a rule turns a metric into a new server count, why scaling down waits, and where a forecast helps.

terms.definition: One running copy of a service. More replicas share the load, and each replica handles a smaller part of it.
How busy a server's processor is, as a share of what it can do. 50 percent means it is half busy.
A number measured over time, such as CPU use or requests per second.

before.note: Load Balancing is the one topic this builds on, because new copies only help once traffic is spread across them. The stages below explain the rest.

stages.name: Basics
body: Scaling a workload means changing how much capacity it has. Kubernetes describes two ways: change the number of replicas, which is horizontal scaling, or change the resources each replica gets, which is vertical scaling [[k8s-autoscaling]].

You can do either by hand, or you can let a controller do it for you. Automatic scaling lets a cluster follow changes in demand more elastically and efficiently than a fixed number would [[k8s-autoscaling]].

AWS describes the same idea for virtual machines: a target tracking policy keeps a chosen metric near a chosen target value, much as a thermostat holds a temperature [[aws-target-tracking]]. If the metric climbs above the target, the group scales out. If it falls below, the group scales in [[aws-target-tracking]].

terms.definition: Giving each replica more or fewer resources.
The value of a metric that the autoscaler tries to hold, such as 50 percent CPU.

stages.name: How it works
body: Kubernetes runs horizontal pod autoscaling as a control loop that runs at intervals, not continuously. The default interval is 15 seconds [[k8s-hpa]]. In each pass, the controller reads the metrics named in the autoscaler definition, finds the Pods of the target, and takes the mean across them [[k8s-hpa]].

For CPU, the utilization is a percentage of what each Pod requested, so a Pod with no CPU request gives no usable value and the autoscaler takes no action on that metric [[k8s-hpa]]. A metrics source is needed too: the resource metrics API is usually provided by an add-on called Metrics Server, which has to be installed separately [[k8s-hpa]].

The core rule is a ratio. The desired replica count is the current count multiplied by the current metric value over the desired value, rounded up [[k8s-hpa]]. If the current value is double the target, the count doubles, and if it is half, the count halves [[k8s-hpa]].

Two guards keep the loop calm. If the ratio is close to 1.0, within a tolerance that is 0.1 by default, no scaling happens [[k8s-hpa]]. And scale-downs use a stabilization window: the controller records its recommendations and takes the highest one from the window, which defaults to 5 minutes, so scale-downs are gradual [[k8s-hpa]].

The vertical autoscaler works differently. A recommender studies current and past usage and stores a target recommendation with a lower and an upper bound. An updater can evict Pods so they are recreated with new requests, or resize them in place where the cluster supports it, and an admission controller applies the recommended values to new Pods [[k8s-vpa]].

AWS adds forecasting. Predictive scaling analyzes historical load to find daily or weekly patterns, forecasts the capacity needed, and raises capacity ahead of the load. AWS says this helps when traffic is cyclical or when applications take a long time to initialize, whereas dynamic scaling is reactive [[aws-predictive]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Starting Pods are a trap for a CPU rule. A Pod that has just started can show misleading high CPU, for instance a Java app warming up. So the Kubernetes controller sets aside Pods that are not yet ready, and it ignores CPU samples from the initialization period, which defaults to 5 minutes, unless the Pod is Ready and the sample was taken while it was Ready [[k8s-hpa]]. When it still would scale up, it assumes the not-yet-ready Pods use none of the desired amount, which softens a scale-up [[k8s-hpa]].

AWS handles the same trouble with an instance warmup. Until the warmup ends, a new instance is not counted toward the group's aggregated metrics, and instances still warming up count toward the desired capacity of the next scale-out so the group does not add more than needed [[aws-target-tracking]]. While a scale-out is in progress, scale-in actions are blocked until warmup ends [[aws-target-tracking]].

Several metrics can be combined. In Kubernetes, the controller computes a desired count for each metric and takes the largest [[k8s-hpa]]. AWS scales out if any target tracking policy is ready to scale out, and scales in only if all of them are ready to scale in [[aws-target-tracking]]. Both choices favour availability.

Vertical autoscaling has update modes. In Off mode the recommender still writes recommendations but nothing is applied. Initial sets requests only when Pods are created. Recreate evicts Pods whose requests differ much from the recommendation. InPlaceOrRecreate tries a resize without restarting and falls back to eviction [[k8s-vpa]].

Whole numbers cause small gaps. AWS notes that because it rounds up when adding and avoids a scale-in that could cause oscillation, a small group can sit visibly away from its target value [[aws-target-tracking]].

terms.definition: The time a new instance needs before its readings should count.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Setting the target is a trade. AWS advises a target as high as possible while leaving a reasonable buffer for unexpected traffic, so resources are used efficiently [[aws-target-tracking]]. A higher target saves money and leaves less room while new capacity starts.

Reactive and predictive scaling cover different cases. AWS says predictive scaling suits cyclical traffic, recurring on-and-off workloads such as batch jobs, and applications that are slow to initialize, and that it can save money by avoiding over-provisioning [[aws-predictive]]. Reactive rules remain the safety net for what no pattern predicts.

Horizontal and vertical scaling are not the same cost. Vertical changes can mean restarting a Pod, and the Kubernetes VPA page notes that in-place resizing depends on cluster support [[k8s-vpa]]. Horizontal scaling needs a workload that can run several copies side by side.
Check the numbers on the topic page's two posts for real fleets: Google's Autopilot paper and MongoDB's predictive auto-scaling experiment show how these ideas behave at scale.

misconceptions.myth: An autoscaler reacts to every change in the metric straight away.
misconceptions.truth: Kubernetes checks on an interval, 15 seconds by default, skips changes inside a tolerance of 0.1 by default, and applies scale-downs using the highest recommendation of a 5 minute window [[k8s-hpa]].

misconceptions.myth: Scaling on CPU works for any Pod.
misconceptions.truth: The HPA computes CPU utilization against the Pod's CPU request, so a container with no request leaves the value undefined and the autoscaler takes no action on that metric [[k8s-hpa]].

AWS describes predictive scaling as proactive and dynamic scaling as reactive, and says to use predictive scaling when there are regular patterns or slow start-up [[aws-predictive]]. Other situations, such as a one-off spike, still rely on the reactive rule.
